query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by the synchronization of precursor reduction rates through a tailored thermal profile. When reduction occurs simultaneously via a rapid heating and cooling cycle, elemental nuclei form concurrently, limiting atomic diffusion and preventing phase segregation. In contrast, a thermal treatment that promotes sequential reduction fosters phase separation and uncontrolled morphology.
generation.material_initial_state: A solid, mixed precursor comprising noble metal salts or complexes uniformly distributed on a support (or in a homogeneous mixture) prior to thermal treatment.
generation.intervention: Adjusting the thermal profile to achieve a rapid (high heating rate and short dwell time) heated‐pulse followed by fast cooling, in comparison to an unaltered (slower or prolonged) thermal ramp.
generation.conditions: Identical precursor composition, concentration, and support characteristics. The only variable change is in the thermal treatment parameters that control reduction kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: The reduction kinetics mediates atomic mixing. Rapid, simultaneous reduction creates a high density of nucleation sites that ‘freeze’ the random, high-entropy configuration, thus leading to a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
generation.mechanism: By shortening the time window for atomic diffusion, the rapid thermal treatment forces all the elements to reduce nearly concurrently. This minimizes differences in their reduction potentials and prevents elemental segregation, as limited surface mobility restricts atom rearrangement that could otherwise lead to phase separation or uncontrolled morphology.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the optimized fast thermal profile, the nanoparticles will display a homogeneous solid-solution structure with high surface atom exposure and uniform elemental distribution, whereas the unchanged slower thermal profile will show evidence of phase separation (or elemental segregation) and less controlled morphology.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized under standard processing conditions (i.e. slower heating or longer dwell times) where sequential reduction of elements is more likely, resulting in phase-separated or compositionally segregated particles.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticle systems synthesized from multielement solid precursors under conditions where thermal reduction kinetics dictate the mixing behavior. It may not apply to synthesis routes dominated by entirely different reduction mechanisms (e.g., purely solution-based chemical reduction) or systems where the reduction potentials of the constituent metals are nearly identical.
generation.uncertainty: The precise values of the heating rate, dwell time, and cooling rate required to achieve synchronous reduction may depend on the specific precursor chemistry and elemental combinations. Additionally, interactions unique to certain metal pairs might necessitate further tuning beyond general rapid thermal treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform two parallel syntheses of noble metal multielement precursor samples under identical conditions except for the thermal treatment. In one experiment, apply a rapid heating pulse with an exceedingly short dwell time and fast cooling (to promote synchronous reduction), while in the control use a slower ramp and longer dwell time expected to induce sequential reduction. All other synthesis variables (composition, atmosphere, support) must be held constant.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm single-phase alloy formation versus phase-segregated phases.
High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) and elemental mapping (e.g., EDX) to evaluate the homogeneity of elemental distribution.
Surface area measurements to reflect differences in particle morphology and atomic exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid thermal treatment does not yield significantly more homogeneous, single-phase HEA nanoparticles compared to the slower treatment (i.e., both conditions show similar levels of phase separation or segregation), then the hypothesis that rapid, synchronized reduction governs alloy homogeneity is falsified.

Due to the difficulties in mixing different elements with various atomic radii, oxidation states, and chemical valence as well as the chemical and physical properties, high entropy materials have great challenges to obtain specimens with a homogeneous structure. The carbothermal shock method was developed to synthesize high entropy alloy nanoparticles composed of more than five elements by a flash heating and cooling process. In addition, an aerosol droplet-mediated technique was employed to synthesize the HEA nanoparticles with atomic-level mixing of immiscible metal elements. Flame spray pyrolysis (FSP) route was also used to produce single-phase (Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn)3(O)4 quinary HEO NPs. These HEA NPs were generated during the fast heating/quenching process, which resulted in the decomposition of the metal precursors and freezing-in of the zero-valent metal atoms simultaneously. These one-step HEO NP syntheses need rapid heating at high temperatures (∼2000 K for the carbothermal shock method, ∼1100 °C for the aerosol synthesis method, and ∼1900 °C for the FSP method) in a short time. These methods have a high requirement for the equipment to achieve fast heating and cooling rate

Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. The elements in CrMnFeCoNi and MnFeCoNiCu HEA NPs also have near equimolar ratios (Supplementary Table 11): Cr (20.2%), Mn (20.4%), Fe (20.7%), Co (20.3%), and Ni (18.4%) for CrMnFeCoNi HEA-H2; Mn (17.8%), Fe (22.4%), Co (21.6%), Ni (19.2%), and Cu (18.9%) for MnFeCoNiCu HEA-H2. On the other hand, the EDX elemental maps of CrFeCoNiCu HEA NPs indicate Cu segregation at the edges of particles while other elements of Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni are homogeneously distributed (Fig. 6i–l). This is attributable to the high positive binary mixing enthalpies between Cu and other elements, especially Cr and Fe (Supplementary Table 7). Similar observations have been reported in other HEA synthesis methods (e.g., arc discharge) and other HEA systems of AlCrFeCoCu and CoCrFeNiCuAl.

These methods require high reaction temperatures, and rapid cooling to maintain a high-entropy state at room temperature. As a result, the preparation of high-entropy nanoparticles with a single solid solution can be achieved in a non-equilibrium state by suppressing the formation of secondary phases. In 2018, a carbothermal shock method was reported by Yao et al. to alloy up to eight elements into HEA NPs with the designated composition and size. This method involves a 55-ms heating of mixed metal precursors on carbon supports at a peak temperature of 2000 K in argon and cooling at a cooling rate of ∼105 K/s. The high temperature ensures uniform mixtures of multiple elements by fission/fusion and catalytically driven particle dispersion mechanisms. This work has made an important step in the rapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles. However, this method can only be applied to conductive, surface-oxidized carbon support materials. Since then, more work has been reported on the rapid synthesis of HEA NPs within milliseconds to seconds, including fast-moving bed heating, electrical sparkling, Joule heating and microwave heating.
